lessons.title: Concepts: templates that explain themselves
lessons.goal: Constrain a template so bad types fail with a readable error.
explain: A concept names a requirement on a type. std::integral<T> is true when T is a whole number; you can combine concepts with || and && to make your own.

Writing template <Numeric T> instead of template <typename T> means the compiler checks the requirement at the call site and says 'constraints not satisfied', instead of dumping twenty lines from inside the body.

example.title: A numeric-only function
notes: names a requirement other code can reuse
checked at compile time, costs nothing at run time

options: Fails to compile: constraints not satisfied
predict.why: std::string is not integral or floating point, so the constraint rejects it before any body is compiled.

quiz.q: What is a concept?
options: A named compile-time requirement on a type
quiz.why: It is a predicate on types evaluated during compilation, used to constrain templates.

quiz.q: Why are constrained templates easier to debug?
options: The error names the unmet requirement instead of the body
quiz.why: The check happens at the call site, so the message points at your argument, not at line 40 of the template.

quiz.q: What does static_assert do?
options: Checks a condition at compile time and stops the build if false
Prints a message at run time
quiz.why: It is evaluated by the compiler and has zero run-time cost.

activity.goal: Write a concept HasSize that is true for anything with a .size() method, and a template T describe(const T&) returning "big" when size() > 3, else "small".
hints: A concept can test an expression: requires(T t) { t.size(); }
The function returns std::string and compares value.size() with 3.
template <HasSize T> std::string describe(const T& value) { return value.size() > 3 ? "big" : "small"; }

lessons.mistake: Writing a concept that is so broad it accepts almost everything - a constraint that never rejects anything gives none of the error-message benefit.
lessons.recap: Concepts turn template requirements into compiled checks with clear messages.

lessons.title: Ranges and views
lessons.goal: Filter and transform a collection without writing loops or copies.
explain: A view is a lightweight, lazy description of a sequence: filter, transform, take. Nothing is computed until you iterate, and nothing is copied.
The pipe syntax reads left to right: scores | views::filter(...) | views::transform(...). It replaces the begin/end pairs and the temporary vectors that old algorithms needed.

example.title: Grades from scores
notes: keeps only elements the predicate accepts
the pipeline is evaluated during the loop

predict.q: How many elements are read from scores by the second loop?
options: Three - take stops requesting after the third
predict.why: take(3) ends the pipeline after three elements, which is the point of lazy views.

quiz.q: What is a view?
options: A lazy, non-owning description of a sequence
quiz.why: Views refer to the original range and compute on demand.

quiz.q: Why must the underlying container outlive the view?
options: The view refers to it and does not own it
quiz.why: A view over destroyed data is a dangling range - the same lifetime rule as references.

quiz.q: Which is equivalent to views::take(n)?
quiz.why: take keeps the first n; drop would skip the first n.

activity.goal: From a list of words, keep those longer than 3 letters, uppercase them, and print them space separated.
hints: Build a pipeline: words | views::filter(...) | views::transform(...)
The transform lambda takes const std::string& and returns a new uppercase string.
Use a small loop inside the lambda, or std::transform from <algorithm>.

lessons.mistake: Building a view over a temporary container, or storing a view and using it after the underlying vector was resized.
lessons.recap: Ranges describe work lazily; nothing runs until you iterate.

lessons.title: Threads and mutexes
lessons.goal: Run work in parallel without corrupting shared data.
explain: std::thread starts a function on another core. The program does not wait for it: you must call join() before the thread object is destroyed, or the program terminates.

Two threads writing the same variable at once is a data race - undefined behaviour, even if it usually 'works'. A std::mutex with std::lock_guard serialises the critical section, and the guard releases the lock automatically.

example.title: Four threads, one counter
notes: starts work on another thread immediately
locks at construction, unlocks at the end of the block
waits for that thread to finish - required before destruction
exactly 4000 because every increment is protected

predict.q: What would counter print if you removed the lock_guard?
options: Usually less than 4000, varying between runs
predict.why: Concurrent read-modify-write loses updates. It is undefined behaviour, so any value is legal - and it may even print 4000 by luck.

quiz.q: What happens if a std::thread is destroyed without join or detach?
quiz.why: The standard refuses to guess: destructing a joinable thread terminates the program.

quiz.q: Why is lock_guard preferred over manual lock/unlock?
options: It unlocks on every exit path, including exceptions
quiz.why: It is RAII for mutexes - the unlock cannot be forgotten.

quiz.q: What is a data race?
options: Two threads reading the same constant
Two threads accessing the same memory with at least one write and no synchronisation
A thread that runs too fast
quiz.why: It is undefined behaviour, which is why the result can change between runs and compilers.

activity.goal: Start three threads that each add 10 to a shared total under a mutex, join them, and print the total.
hints: The lambda captures by reference: [&]() { ... }
Inside: std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m); total += 10;
Store the threads in a vector, then join every one before printing.

lessons.mistake: Holding a lock while doing slow work (I/O, sleeping), which serialises everything and removes the benefit of threads.
lessons.recap: Threads run concurrently; a mutex makes the shared part safe.

lessons.title: async and future
lessons.goal: Start work now and collect the result when you need it.
explain: std::async runs a function asynchronously and hands back a std::future - a placeholder for a result that may not exist yet. Calling get() waits only if the work is still running.
Launch policy matters: std::launch::async guarantees a new thread; without it the implementation may defer the work until get(), which is not what you want when you are trying to overlap tasks.

example.title: Two seconds of work, overlapped
notes: starts immediately on a new thread
waits for the result, or returns it if ready
it moves the value out - calling it again throws std::future_error

predict.q: When does the 20 ms sleep happen?
predict.why: With launch::async the work starts right away, so the sleep overlaps with the printing of 'started'.

quiz.q: What does future::get() do?
options: Waits for and returns the result, then invalidates the future
quiz.why: get() blocks until the value exists. Calling it twice on the same future is an error; the value must be cached first.

quiz.q: Why pass std::launch::async explicitly?
options: Otherwise the work may be deferred until get(), so nothing overlaps
quiz.why: The default policy lets the implementation choose, including deferring.

quiz.q: What is a data race's relationship to async?
options: Tasks may run on another thread, so shared data still needs protection
quiz.why: async moves work to a thread; it does not add synchronisation to your variables.

activity.goal: Launch two async tasks that return 10 and 32, call get() on both, and print their sum.
hints: auto a = std::async(std::launch::async, value, 10);
The second is the same call with 32.
Print a.get() + b.get() - both must be called.

lessons.mistake: Letting a future go out of scope without calling get() - with launch::async the destructor blocks until the task finishes, which can look like a mystery hang.
lessons.recap: async starts work, future carries the result, get() waits only when needed.

lessons.title: Measuring performance
lessons.goal: Measure how long code takes, and avoid believing a single run.
explain: std::chrono::steady_clock is monotonic, which is what you want for durations: it cannot jump backwards like the wall clock can.

Measure a loop that runs many times, not one call, and run it several times. First runs are slower (cold caches, page faults), and a release build with optimisation can be ten times faster than a debug build.

example.title: Timing a vector build
notes: converts the difference to a plain number
a stable claim; the exact time would change every run

predict.q: Why does this example print a comparison instead of the microseconds?
options: The exact time changes every run, so an exact expected output would be wrong
Because us is not a number
predict.why: A lesson that claims an exact duration would fail on a faster machine - the check must be a property, not a number.

quiz.q: Why steady_clock rather than system_clock?
options: It never jumps backwards, so durations are meaningful
It is the only one that compiles
quiz.why: system_clock can be adjusted by the operating system, which corrupts a measurement.

quiz.q: Why run the measured code many times?
options: Timers are noisy and single fast operations are lost in that noise
quiz.why: Measuring 200000 iterations gives a signal much larger than the timer's resolution.

quiz.q: What does -O0 versus -O2 change?
options: The machine code, often by a large factor
quiz.why: Optimisation is why you should benchmark a release build - a debug build measures the compiler's generosity, not your algorithm.

activity.goal: Time two loops of 100000 iterations: one appending to a vector without reserve, one with reserve. Print the sizes and whether both finished under a second.
hints: Wrap each loop in its own pair of now() calls.
reserve(N) before the loop avoids repeated reallocation.
Convert with duration_cast<microseconds> and compare both with 1000000.

lessons.mistake: Benchmarking a debug build, or timing a single call and drawing conclusions from noise.
lessons.recap: Measure with steady_clock, measure in bulk, and only trust comparisons.

lessons.title: Project organisation and build checks
lessons.goal: Make the build fail loudly when the standard or feature is wrong.
explain: A real project states its requirements in the build file: the C++ standard, warnings, and the sources. CMake is the common choice; the compiler flags matter more than the tool.
You can also assert requirements in code. static_assert(__cplusplus >= 202002L) turns 'this needs C++20' into a build error with your own message instead of a wall of syntax errors.

example.title: Asking the compiler what it supports
notes: a compile-time check with your own error text
feature macros let you support two standards from one file

predict.q: What happens if you build this file with -std=c++17?
options: It fails on the static_assert with your message
predict.why: 201703 < 202002, so the assertion fires at compile time and the build stops with 'This course needs C++20 or newer'.

quiz.q: Why put the standard in the build file rather than a comment?
options: The build then enforces it for every file
quiz.why: A requirement in prose is a suggestion; one in the build is a rule.

quiz.q: What does __cplusplus report?
options: The standard the compiler is using, as a number
quiz.why: It is the language standard macro: 199711, 201103, 201703, 202002.

quiz.q: Which is a feature-test macro?
quiz.why: Feature macros like __cpp_lib_ranges exist only when the feature is present, which makes them safe to test with #ifdef.

activity.goal: Add a static_assert that sizeof(int) is 4, then print __cplusplus.
hints: static_assert(sizeof(int) == 4, "int must be 4 bytes");
The macro is printed like any number: std::cout << __cplusplus;
Remember the newline.

lessons.mistake: Relying on a compiler default standard. Always state -std=c++20 (or the CMake equivalent) so the code means the same thing everywhere.
lessons.recap: Put requirements in the build and in static_assert, so they cannot be forgotten.

lessons.title: Capstone 1: designing the classes
lessons.goal: Turn a fuzzy requirement into classes with clear responsibilities.
explain: A mission planner needs a Task (data), a Planner (rules), and a way to ask 'what next?'. Each class does one job, and the Planner owns its tasks - no global state.
next() returns std::optional<Task>: there may genuinely be nothing left to do, and the type says so instead of returning a fake task.

example.title: planner.cpp - the core
example.output:
remaining 3
next charge
then calibrate
left 2
notes: plain data, no behaviour - easy to copy and print
owns the vector and enforces the rules
there may be nothing left, and the type says so
a pointer to the existing task, no copying

predict.q: What does next() return after all three tasks are completed?
options: A Task with an empty title
predict.why: Every task is done, so no candidate is found and the optional is empty - the caller must handle it.

quiz.q: Why is Task a struct rather than a class?
options: It is passive data with no invariant to protect
Classes cannot be stored in vectors
quiz.why: Use a struct for plain bundles and a class when you need to enforce rules.

quiz.q: Why does Planner own the tasks instead of exposing the vector?
options: So nothing outside can break 'done' or bypass the ordering rule
Because vectors are private by default
quiz.why: Ownership is what lets the class keep its promises.

quiz.q: What is the cost of returning std::optional<Task> by value?
options: One copy of the task, which is small
quiz.why: The optional holds a Task inline; copying a small struct is cheap and safe.

activity.goal: Add a count_done() method returning how many tasks are finished, and print it after completing two tasks.
hints: count_done uses std::count_if with [](const Task& t) { return t.done; }.
Cast the result to int if you return int.
Complete both by title, then print "done " << p.count_done().

lessons.mistake: Letting the UI, the storage and the rules live in one class. Split by responsibility and each part becomes testable.
lessons.recap: Design is deciding who owns what and what each class promises.

lessons.title: Capstone 2: a test harness and the finish
lessons.goal: Wire the planner into a tiny test harness so the rules stay true.
explain: A test harness runs checks and counts failures instead of stopping at the first one, so you see every broken rule in one run. Returning a non-zero exit code lets a script or CI decide pass or fail.
Keep the checks small and named. 'add positive' tells you what broke; 'test 3' does not.

example.title: harness.cpp
notes: records the result instead of aborting
you see every failure in one run
the exit code is what a script reads

predict.q: If add had a bug, what would the program print and return?
options: A FAIL line, then a summary with failures above zero, and exit code 1
predict.why: The harness keeps going: each failing check prints its name, the summary counts them, and main returns 1.

quiz.q: Why count failures instead of stopping at the first?
options: One run shows every broken rule
quiz.why: Fixing one failure at a time hides the rest; a summary shows the shape of the problem.

quiz.q: Why does the exit code matter?
options: Scripts and CI read it to decide whether the build passed
It is printed to the user
quiz.why: Exit code 0 means success; anything else fails the pipeline.

quiz.q: What makes a good test name?
options: A short statement of the rule being checked
quiz.why: The name is the only clue you get when it fails at 2am.

activity.goal: Use the harness to check two rules of a Wallet: withdrawing more than the balance fails, and a valid withdrawal lowers the balance.
hints: Create a Wallet w{100};
check(!w.withdraw(150), "overdraw refused");
check(w.withdraw(40) && w.balance() == 60, "valid withdrawal");

lessons.mistake: Writing tests that only exercise the happy path. The guard you never test is the one that quietly stops working.
lessons.recap: A harness that counts failures is the cheapest safety net a project can have.
